newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU wants to phase out Nordic alcohol quotas.
newsitem.headline: EU wants to phase out Nordic alcohol quotas.

text.p: The European Commission proposed on Wednesday that Nordic European Union members Denmark, Finland and Sweden phase out their limits on the amount of alcohol and cigarettes that travellers may bring home by June 30, 2002.
The move, which was expected, puts the EU executive on a collision course with Sweden, which argues that its restrictions on personal alcohol imports are vital for its social and health policies.
Finance Minister Erik Asbrink threatened to veto the proposal and indicated that Stockholm was prepared to defend itself in the EU court, which may end up settling the issue.
"We will not accept the proposal," Asbrink told the Swedish news agency TT in Stockholm.
Sweden would try to get the other EU countries to take a different position from the Commission, he said.
EU finance ministers will debate the issue on December 2.
EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said on Wednesday he was ready to take account of the difficulties of the Nordic states by giving them a transition period to adapt their policies.
But the quotas must end because they violated a fundamental principle of the EU's single market -- the right of citizens to carry goods for their personal use freely across its borders.

The Commission said it had proposed that the three countries immediately reduce the minimum period that travellers must be away to qualify for tax exemptions on alcohol and tobacco from 36 hours to 24 hours.
The question of alcohol quotas is sensitive for the Nordic states, which have traditionally applied high taxes to alcohol and tobacco to discourage consumption and raise revenue.
Alcohol and tobacco taxes bring in about $2.7 billion annually in Sweden and $2.17 billion in Finland.
As Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict the flow.
However, last month it became clear that the Nordics were split on the issue.
Sweden continued to insist it could not accept any deadline for ending the restrictions while both Finland and Denmark indicated they could accept a final date.
However, Finland will seek six more months for phasing out its restrictions, the Finnish news agency reported on Wednesday.
Asbrink said Sweden wanted the current rules to continue to apply for some years. "Then we will sit down again and discuss the future," he said.
The EU executive has said the Nordic exemptions to EU rules, which allow them to restrict alcohol imports, were due to expire by the end of 1996 unless there was a new agreement.
A Swede is currently allowed to take home one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer compared with 10, 90 and 110 litres respectively for other EU citizens.
